title: Black Bean, Corn, and Rice Burrito Bowls with Quick-Pickled Red Onion
description: Cumin-scented black beans, lime rice, corn, and salsa, built in containers so they reheat without turning to mush. The pickled onion keeps everything bright on day four. About $1.75 a bowl.
notes: Pack the rice and beans together in the bottom of each container, then corn and salsa on top, and keep the pickled onion and any avocado in a small separate cup so they stay crisp and bright. Everything but the avocado keeps 4 days in the refrigerator; slice avocado the morning you eat it. Reheat the bowl, uncovered with the onion removed, in the microwave for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring once, until it reaches 165°F, then add the cold toppings back. Brown rice works in place of white; it needs about 45 minutes and 2 cups of water. Canned beans are the quick route, but 1 cup of dried black beans simmered until tender replaces the two cans for about a third of the price. The pickled onion keeps 2 weeks on its own and is good on sandwiches and eggs. Refrigerate the cooked components within 2 hours of cooking.

ingredients.name: long grain white rice (190 g), rinsed until the water runs clear
medium red onion, halved and very thinly sliced
black beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
tomato salsa or pico de gallo
ripe avocado, sliced the day you eat it

instructions: Combine the rinsed rice, water, and 1/2 teaspoon of the salt in a medium saucepan. Bring to a boil over high heat, then cover, reduce the heat to the lowest setting, and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork and stir in the lime zest and half the lime juice.

While the rice cooks, make the pickled onion. Put the sliced red onion in a small heatproof bowl or jar. Warm the vinegar, sugar, 1/4 teaspoon of the salt, and 1/3 cup water in a small pan or the microwave until steaming, pour it over the onion, and press the slices under the liquid. Set aside; it turns pink and softens in about 20 minutes.
Heat the olive oil in a 10-inch skillet over medium heat. Add the garlic, cumin, chili powder, and oregano and stir for 30 seconds, until fragrant but not browned.

Add the black beans, 1/2 cup water, and the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Simmer for 5 to 6 minutes, mashing about a quarter of the beans against the side of the pan with a spoon so the liquid thickens and coats the rest. Stir in the remaining lime juice and take the pan off the heat.
Rinse the frozen corn under hot tap water in a strainer for about 1 minute until thawed, then shake it dry. This keeps it sweet and firm rather than cooking it twice.

Divide the rice among 4 containers, spoon the beans over one side, and add the corn and salsa beside them. Let the containers cool, uncovered, for 20 to 30 minutes before lidding. Pack the drained pickled onion and the cilantro in a small separate cup for each bowl, and add avocado the morning you eat it.

title: Egg Soboro Rice Box with Sesame Spinach and Soy-Glazed Carrot
description: A Japanese-style three-color lunch box: sweet-salty scrambled egg crumbles, sesame-dressed spinach, and glazed carrot over short-grain rice. Eggs make it the cheapest protein in the kitchen, about $1.50 a box.
notes: Stirring the eggs constantly with chopsticks or a whisk over low heat is what turns them into fine, dry crumbles instead of a scramble; take the pan off the heat the moment they stop looking wet. Japanese short-grain rice is the point here because it stays tender when cold, but any white rice works. Swap gluten-free tamari for the soy sauce and the box is gluten-free. The boxes keep 3 days in the refrigerator and are good cold or reheated 90 seconds in the microwave until steaming (165°F). Add the crumbled seaweed only when you eat, or it goes limp. Refrigerate the packed boxes within 2 hours of cooking, and keep a cold pack with a lunch that will sit out past an hour.

ingredients.name: japanese short-grain rice (300 g), rinsed until the water runs nearly clear
roasted seasoned seaweed snack sheets, crumbled

instructions: Put the rinsed rice and water in a medium saucepan and let it soak for 15 minutes while you prepare everything else. Bring to a boil over high heat, cover, reduce to the lowest heat, and cook for 13 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more, then fluff gently.
Crack the eggs into a bowl and whisk them with 1 1/2 tablespoons of the sugar, 1 tablespoon of the soy sauce, and 1/4 teaspoon of the salt until no streaks remain.

Heat 1 teaspoon of the neutral oil in a 10-inch nonstick skillet over medium-low heat. Pour in the eggs and immediately begin stirring with four chopsticks held together or a whisk, scraping the bottom constantly. Cook for 4 to 6 minutes, lowering the heat if they catch, until the eggs break into small, dry, pale-yellow crumbles. Scrape them onto a plate.

Wipe the skillet, add the remaining 2 teaspoons oil, and set it over medium heat. Add the carrot matchsticks and cook, tossing, for 3 minutes until just bendable. Add 1 tablespoon soy sauce and the remaining 1/2 tablespoon sugar and cook for 1 minute more, until the liquid cooks down to a glaze. Move the carrots to the plate.

Add the spinach to the same skillet with 2 tablespoons water, cover, and steam over medium heat for 2 minutes, until wilted. Tip it into a strainer, press out as much water as you can with the back of a spoon, and roughly chop. Toss with the remaining 1 tablespoon soy sauce, the sesame seeds, sesame oil, and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt.

Divide the rice among 4 lunch boxes and press it level. Arrange the egg crumbles over one half and the spinach and carrots over the other, so each box shows three colors. Scatter with scallions, cool uncovered for 20 minutes, then lid and refrigerate. Add the crumbled seaweed at the table.

title: Lemongrass Tofu Rice Noodle Jars with Lime-Chile Dressing
description: A Vietnamese bún-style noodle salad layered in jars: dressing at the bottom, crisp vegetables, seared lemongrass tofu, noodles, and herbs on top. Shake and eat cold. About $2.25 a jar.
equipment: 4 wide-mouth quart jars or deep containers
clean kitchen towel for pressing tofu
notes: Press the tofu well, since dry slabs brown and soak up the marinade instead of steaming. Only the tender, pale lower third of the lemongrass stalk is soft enough to mince; freeze the rest for broth. The layering order matters: dressing on the bottom, then carrots and cucumber, then tofu, noodles, and herbs, so nothing above the vegetables sits in liquid. Jars keep 4 days in the refrigerator; tip into a bowl and toss, or shake with the lid on. Leave out the peanuts for a nut-free lunch, or pack them in a twist of paper to add at the end so they stay crunchy. Fish sauce is traditional in the dressing in place of tamari if you are not keeping it vegan (it adds the fish allergen). Keep the jars cold with an ice pack if lunch is more than an hour away, and eat them cold rather than reheating.

ingredients.name: extra-firm tofu, pressed for 15 minutes and cut into 1/2-inch-thick slabs
lemongrass stalk, tough outer layers removed, tender lower part finely minced (about 2 tbsp)
serrano or green chile, very thinly sliced
english cucumber, halved lengthwise, seeded, and cut into matchsticks

instructions: Pat the pressed tofu slabs dry and lay them in a shallow dish. Stir together the lemongrass, two-thirds of the garlic, 2 tablespoons of the tamari, the brown sugar, and the salt, and spoon it over both sides of the tofu. Let it sit for 15 minutes while you cook the noodles and cut the vegetables.

Bring a large pot of water to a boil. Add the rice noodles, stir, and cook for 4 to 6 minutes, until tender with no chalky center. Drain, rinse under cold water until fully cool, and shake dry; cold rinsing is what keeps them from clumping in the jar.

Make the dressing by stirring the lime juice, water, granulated sugar, the remaining 2 tablespoons tamari, the remaining garlic, and the sliced chile together until the sugar dissolves. Taste; it should be sharp, sweet, and salty in equal measure.

Heat the oil in a 12-inch nonstick skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lift the tofu out of the marinade, letting the bits of lemongrass cling, and lay the slabs in the pan. Cook for 4 to 5 minutes per side without moving them, until deeply browned at the edges. Spoon any remaining marinade over the tofu in the last minute. Cool, then cut into strips.
Build the jars: 3 tablespoons dressing in the bottom of each, then carrots, cucumber, and sprouts, then the tofu strips, then a loose nest of noodles. Top with the mint and cilantro and seal.
Refrigerate until lunch. To eat, turn the jar upside down into a bowl or shake it hard for a few seconds with the lid on, then add the peanuts.

title: Roasted Spiced Chickpea Pita Pockets with Cucumber-Yogurt Sauce
description: Chickpeas roasted with cumin, coriander, and paprika until crisp-edged, packed into pita with a garlicky cucumber-yogurt sauce, tomatoes, and romaine. Assemble at lunch so the bread stays soft. About $2 a pocket.
notes: Dry the chickpeas thoroughly on a towel before roasting; wet chickpeas steam and never crisp. The sauce is a quick tzatziki-style sauce, and squeezing the grated cucumber hard is what keeps it thick enough to spread. Pack the chickpeas, sauce, and vegetables in separate compartments and the pita in a bag, then fill the pita at lunch; pre-filled pockets go soggy in an hour. Chickpeas keep 4 days refrigerated and soften as they sit, so re-crisp them for 5 minutes in a 400°F oven or a dry skillet if you are home, or eat them as they are. A plain dairy-free yogurt made from coconut makes the sauce dairy-free and the whole recipe vegan. Refrigerate the sauce within 2 hours of making it and keep a cold pack with the lunch.

ingredients.name: chickpeas (15 oz each), drained, rinsed, and patted very dry
medium red onion, very thinly sliced

instructions: Heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the middle. On a rimmed baking sheet, toss the dried chickpeas with the olive oil, cumin, coriander, smoked paprika, turmeric, garlic powder, cayenne, and 3/4 teaspoon of the salt until evenly coated, and spread them in a single layer.

Roast for 22 to 25 minutes, shaking the pan once halfway, until the chickpeas are golden, slightly shrunken, and crisp on the outside with a creamy center. Let them cool on the pan; they crisp further as they cool.
While the chickpeas roast, put the grated cucumber in a fine-mesh strainer with the remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt, let it sit for 5 minutes, then squeeze it hard in your fist until it stops dripping.
Stir the squeezed cucumber into the yogurt with the grated garlic, lemon juice, and dill. Taste for salt. It should be thick enough to hold a spoon upright.
For packing, divide the cooled chickpeas, sauce, tomatoes, romaine, and onion among containers with separate compartments or small cups, and wrap the pita halves separately.
At lunch, open each pita half, spread a spoonful of sauce inside, and fill with romaine, chickpeas, tomatoes, and onion, finishing with more sauce on top.

title: Chana Aloo Wraps: Spiced Chickpea and Potato Kathi-Roll-Style Rolls
description: A dry-style chickpea and potato curry with cumin seed, ginger, and garam masala, rolled in warm tortillas with raw onion and lemon. The filling thickens as it cools, so the wraps hold together for days. About $1.60 a wrap.
notes: Kathi rolls are usually made with paratha; a large flour tortilla is the closest cheap, widely available stand-in. The filling should be nearly dry when you roll it, with no liquid pooling, or the wrap will leak. Rolled wraps keep 4 days refrigerated and freeze well for 2 months wrapped in foil; reheat a refrigerated wrap in its foil in a 375°F oven for 12 minutes, or unwrapped in the microwave for 90 seconds, until the center reaches 165°F, and reheat a frozen one in the oven for 25 minutes. Use corn tortillas for a gluten-free version and make smaller rolls. Add a spoonful of plain yogurt inside if you are not keeping it vegan (adds milk). Cool the filling within 2 hours of cooking.

ingredients.name: russet or yukon gold potatoes (450 g), peeled and cut into 1/2-inch dice
serrano or green chile, finely minced
chickpeas (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
medium red onion, very thinly sliced

instructions: Put the diced potatoes in a 12-inch skillet, add water to cover by 1/2 inch and a big pinch of the salt, and bring to a boil. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, until a fork slides in easily. Drain and set aside; wipe out the skillet.

Heat the oil in the same skillet over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and let them sizzle for 20 seconds, then add the onion and cook, stirring, for 6 to 8 minutes, until soft and golden at the edges.

Stir in the ginger, garlic, and chile and cook for 1 minute. Add the turmeric, coriander, garam masala, cayenne, and tomato paste and stir for 1 minute more, until the paste darkens a shade and smells toasty.

Add the chickpeas, the cooked potatoes, the salt, and the 3/4 cup water. Cover and simmer over medium-low heat for 8 minutes, then uncover and crush about a third of the mixture with a potato masher so it binds together. Cook, stirring, for 3 to 4 minutes more, until almost no liquid remains and the mixture mounds on a spoon.
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the cilantro and lemon juice. Taste for salt. Let the filling cool for 15 minutes so it firms up before rolling.

Warm each tortilla in a dry skillet for 20 seconds per side until pliable. Spread about 3/4 cup of filling in a strip across the lower third, scatter with red onion, fold in the sides, and roll up tightly. Wrap each roll in foil or parchment and refrigerate once cool.

title: Hoppin' John-Style Pinto Beans and Rice with Collards and Bacon
description: A Southern pot of beans, rice, and collards cooked in one pan, seasoned with a few slices of bacon and a splash of vinegar at the end. Four ounces of bacon flavors six lunches, so it comes in around $1.50 a serving.
equipment: large heavy pot or Dutch oven with lid
notes: Hoppin' John is properly made with black-eyed peas; use them if you find them, but pinto beans are usually cheaper and cook the same way here. Keep the heat low once the rice goes in and resist stirring, which makes the rice gummy. The vinegar at the end is not optional in spirit: it wakes up a pot that otherwise tastes flat after a day in the refrigerator. Portions keep 4 days refrigerated and freeze for 3 months; reheat with a spoonful of water, covered, in the microwave for 3 minutes, stirring halfway, until steaming hot (165°F). For a vegetarian version, skip the bacon, cook the vegetables in 2 tablespoons of oil with an extra 1/2 teaspoon smoked paprika, and use vegetable broth. Cool the pot within 2 hours of cooking; spreading it in the containers speeds that up.

ingredients.name: thick-cut bacon (about 4 oz), cut into 1/2-inch pieces
long grain white rice (190 g), rinsed
pinto beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
collard greens (about 10 oz), stems removed, leaves cut into thin ribbons
louisiana-style cayenne pepper hot sauce, for serving

instructions: Put the bacon in a large heavy pot over medium heat and cook, stirring now and then, for 6 to 8 minutes, until browned and most of the fat has rendered. Leave the bacon and about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pot; spoon off any extra.
Add the onion, celery, and bell pepper and cook for 6 minutes, stirring, until softened. Stir in the garlic, smoked paprika, thyme, cayenne, and bay leaf and cook for 1 minute, until fragrant.
Add the rice and stir for 1 minute to coat the grains in the fat. Pour in the broth, add the salt and pepper, and bring to a boil.

Scatter the pinto beans over the top, then pile the collard ribbons on top of the beans without stirring them in; they will steam down. Cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.

Turn off the heat and let the pot stand, covered, for 10 minutes. Remove the bay leaf, add the vinegar, and fold everything together gently from the bottom with a wide spoon. Taste and add salt if needed.
Divide among 6 containers, cool uncovered for 30 minutes, then lid and refrigerate. Pack hot sauce on the side.

title: Olivier-Style Potato Salad with Eggs, Peas, and Dill Pickles
description: The Russian and Eastern European holiday salad, made as a weekday lunch: diced potatoes, carrots, hard-cooked eggs, peas, and pickles folded into a mustardy mayonnaise and sour cream dressing. Keeps four days. About $1.25 a serving.
notes: Cook the potatoes and carrots whole and in their skins, then peel and dice them once cool; they hold their shape and soak up far less water than pre-diced ones. Dice everything to the size of a pea so each forkful has a bit of everything, which is the whole character of this salad. It is better on day two than day one, and keeps 4 days in the refrigerator; it does not freeze. Eat it cold or at cool room temperature, never reheated. Keep it with a cold pack if lunch is more than an hour away, since it contains eggs and mayonnaise, and refrigerate it within 2 hours of making it. For a dairy-free version, replace the sour cream with more mayonnaise.

ingredients.name: yukon gold potato (680 g), scrubbed, left whole
dill pickle chips, drained and finely chopped

instructions: Put the whole potatoes and carrots in a large pot, cover with cold water by 1 inch, and salt the water. Bring to a boil and cook for 18 to 22 minutes, pulling the carrots out after about 12 minutes when a knife slides in easily, and the potatoes when they are tender all the way through. Drain and let cool until you can handle them.

Meanwhile, put the eggs in a medium saucepan, cover with cold water, and bring to a boil. Turn off the heat, cover, and leave for 11 minutes. Move the eggs to a bowl of ice water for 5 minutes, then peel.
Put the frozen peas in a strainer and run hot tap water over them for 1 minute to thaw, then shake dry.
Peel the cooled potatoes and carrots and cut them, with the eggs, into 1/3-inch dice. Put them in a large bowl with the peas, chopped pickles, and scallions.
Stir together the mayonnaise, sour cream, mustard, lemon juice, dill, salt, and pepper. Pour over the bowl and fold gently with a spatula until everything is coated without mashing the potatoes.
Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour so the flavors settle, then taste again for salt before dividing into 6 containers.

title: Jamaican-Style Stew Peas with Coconut Milk, Thyme, and Spinners
description: Kidney beans simmered in coconut milk with scallion, thyme, allspice, and a whole scotch bonnet, with small flour dumplings dropped in at the end. Thick, filling, and better the next day over rice. About $1.40 a serving.
equipment: small bowl for the dumpling dough
notes: Stew peas is traditionally cooked with salted pig tail or beef; this meatless version leans on coconut milk, thyme, and allspice for depth. Keep the scotch bonnet whole and unbroken for aroma without much heat, and fish it out before packing; burst it against the pot if you want it hot. Spinners are rolled from a stiff flour dough, and they thicken the stew as they cook, so add them only when the beans are already tender. Leave them out and the stew is gluten-free. Portions keep 4 days refrigerated and freeze for 3 months (the dumplings soften but hold); reheat covered with a splash of water for 3 to 4 minutes in the microwave, stirring halfway, until steaming hot (165°F). Dried kidney beans are cheaper: use 1 1/2 cups, soaked overnight and simmered until tender, in place of the cans, and reduce the broth to 1 cup. Cool within 2 hours.

ingredients.name: scallions, sliced, white and green parts kept separate
scotch bonnet or habanero chile, left whole
kidney beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed
hot cooked jasmine rice, for serving

instructions: Melt the coconut oil in a large heavy pot over medium heat. Add the onion, garlic, scallion whites, and carrot and cook, stirring, for 6 minutes, until soft. Stir in the thyme sprigs and allspice and cook for 30 seconds.

Add the kidney beans, coconut milk, broth, the whole scotch bonnet, 1 teaspoon of the salt, and the pepper. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low, partly cover, and cook for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally so the bottom does not catch.

While the beans simmer, mix the flour, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt, and the 1/3 cup water in a small bowl into a stiff dough, kneading briefly in the bowl until smooth. Pinch off teaspoon-sized pieces and roll each between your palms into a thin spindle about 2 inches long.

Drop the spinners into the simmering stew, give it one gentle stir, and cook uncovered for 12 to 15 minutes, until the dumplings are firm and cooked through and the stew has thickened enough to coat a spoon. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot if you want it thicker.
Remove the scotch bonnet and thyme stems. Stir in the scallion greens and taste for salt; coconut milk mutes seasoning, so it may need another pinch.
Pack about 2/3 cup rice in each container with a generous ladle of stew beside or over it. Cool uncovered for 30 minutes, then lid and refrigerate.

title: Tuna and Cannellini Bean Salad with Lemon, Parsley, and Red Onion
description: The Italian pantry lunch: canned tuna and white beans tossed with vinegar-softened red onion, celery, tomatoes, parsley, and good olive oil. No cooking, keeps four days, and improves as it sits. About $2.25 a serving.
notes: Soaking the sliced onion in vinegar for 10 minutes takes away its raw bite and seasons the whole salad. Tuna packed in olive oil tastes richer and you can use its oil in the dressing; tuna in water works too, and is often cheaper. Hold back the parsley and tomatoes from any portion you will eat after day two and add them fresh, since they fade first. The salad keeps 4 days refrigerated; it is meant to be eaten cold or at room temperature, not reheated. Pile it over baby greens, scoop it with crackers, or stuff it into a split roll for a sandwich (bread adds wheat). Pack with a cold pack if it will sit out more than an hour, and refrigerate within 2 hours of making it.

ingredients.name: medium red onion, very thinly sliced
tuna (canned) in olive oil or water (5 oz each), drained
cannellini beans (15 oz each), drained and rinsed

instructions: Put the sliced red onion in a small bowl with the red wine vinegar and a pinch of the salt. Toss and let it sit for 10 minutes while you prepare the rest; it will soften and turn pink.
In a large bowl, break the drained tuna into large flakes with a fork. Add the cannellini beans, celery, cherry tomatoes, parsley, and capers.

Add the onion and its vinegar, the olive oil, lemon juice, lemon zest, salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes. Fold gently with a spatula so the beans stay whole and the tuna stays in flakes rather than paste.
Taste and adjust: it usually wants another squeeze of lemon or a pinch more salt, because the beans drink up seasoning. Let it sit for 15 minutes before the first taste if you can.
Divide among 4 containers. Pack the baby greens separately and spoon the salad over them at lunch, or eat it on its own with a fork.

title: Thai-Inspired Basil Turkey Rice Boxes with Green Beans
description: A pad kra pao-style stir-fry of ground turkey with garlic, chiles, green beans, and a big handful of basil, stretched over six boxes of jasmine rice. One pound of turkey feeds six, so it lands around $2.10 a box.
notes: Holy basil is the classic herb and Thai basil the usual substitute; ordinary sweet basil from the grocery store still tastes right here, and stirring it in off the heat keeps it fragrant. Cook the turkey to 165°F, which happens well before it browns; the browning in step 4 is for flavor. The vegetables stretch the meat and keep the boxes lighter. Boxes keep 4 days refrigerated and freeze for 2 months; reheat covered in the microwave for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring once, until steaming hot (165°F). Use gluten-free tamari for the soy sauce to make it gluten-free. A fried egg on top is traditional if you are eating it fresh at home. Cool the boxes within 2 hours of cooking; ground poultry spoils quickly if left warm.

ingredients.name: serrano or green chile, thinly sliced
green beans, trimmed and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
red bell pepper, cut into 1/2-inch dice
fresh basil leaves (about 2 oz), large leaves torn
lime, cut into 6 wedges, for serving

instructions: Combine the rinsed rice and water in a medium saucepan with a pinch of the salt. Bring to a boil, cover, reduce the heat to low, and cook for 15 minutes. Turn off the heat and let it stand, covered, for 10 minutes, then fluff.
Stir together the soy sauce, fish sauce, brown sugar, and 2 tablespoons water in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves, and set it by the stove.
Heat the oil in a 12-inch skillet or wok over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add the garlic and chiles and stir for 20 seconds, until fragrant but not browned.

Add the turkey and the salt, breaking the meat into small pieces with a spatula. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring only now and then so it browns in spots, until no pink remains and the meat reaches 165°F on a thermometer.

Add the green beans and bell pepper and cook, tossing, for 3 to 4 minutes, until the beans are bright green and just tender. Pour in the sauce and cook for 1 minute more, until it reduces to a light glaze.

Take the pan off the heat and fold in the basil until it wilts. Divide the rice among 6 boxes, spoon the turkey over it, and tuck a lime wedge into each. Cool uncovered for 20 minutes, then lid and refrigerate.
